#### 3.2.1. Solving LRA: Linear Real Arithmetic

We provide an outline of Z3's main procedure for solving formulas over linear real arithmetic \[[28](#dutertrem06 "B. Dutertre and L. de Moura. 
A Fast Linear-Arithmetic Solver for DPLL(T).")\]. It maintains a (dual) Simplex tableau that encodes equalities of the form ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,). Feasibility of the equalities depends on bounds, ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,), currently associated with the variables. For the following formula

```
  x, y = Reals('x y')
  solve([x >= 0, Or(x + y <= 2, x + 2*y >= 6), 
                 Or(x + y >= 2, x + 2*y > 4)])
```

Z3 introduces auxiliary variables ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) and represents the formula as

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Only bounds (e.g., ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)) are asserted during search.

The first two equalities form the tableau. Thus, the definitions ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) produce the equalities

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

They are equivalent to the normal form:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

where ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) are basic (dependent) and ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) are non-basic. In dual Simplex tableaux, values of a non-basic variable ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) can be chosen between ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) and ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,). The value of a basic variable is a function of non-basic variable values. It is the unique value that satisfies the unique row where the basic variable occurs. Pivoting swaps basic and non-basic variables and is used to get values of basic variables within bounds. For example, assume we start with a set of initial values ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) and bounds ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,). Then ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) has to be 2 and it is made non-basic. Instead ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) becomes basic:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The new tableau updates the assignment of variables to ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,). The resulting assignment is a model for the original formula.
